# ♟️ Searchless Chess: Master-Level Neural Intuition

This model collection demonstrates that neural networks can develop high-level chess intuition **without any search algorithms** (no minimax, no alpha-beta pruning). By training on millions of positions evaluated by Stockfish, these models learn to predict optimal moves based purely on board patterns.

## 🏆 Model Lineup & Variations

This project includes three distinct architectures to showcase the evolution of neural chess intuition:

| Model | Architecture | Params | ELO | Key Feature |
|-------|--------------|--------|-----|-------------|
| **ViT-Medium** | Vision Transformer | 9.5M | **1960** | **Flagship:** Best performance, master-level play. |
| **ViT-Small** | Vision Transformer | 2.64M | **1817** | **Efficiency:** 10x more parameter-efficient than ResNet. |
| **ResNet-Large** | Convolutional (ResNet) | 12.9M | **1711** | **Baseline:** Traditional deep learning approach. |

---

## 📊 Performance Comparison (Puzzle Accuracy)

Models were evaluated on 1,200 Lichess puzzles across different difficulty tiers:

| Model | Tier 4 (1000-1250) | Tier 6 (1500-1750) | Tier 8 (2000-2250) |
|-------|--------------------|--------------------|--------------------|
| **ViT-Medium** | **88%** | **86%** | **45%** |
| **ViT-Small** | 82% | 68% | 34% |
| **ResNet-Large** | 76% | 59% | 23% |

---

## 🚀 Quick Start & Usage

Each variation includes:
- `model.keras`: Full model (architecture + weights) - **Recommended for Kaggle Notebooks**.
- `model.weights.h5`: Standalone weights.
- `config.json`: Architecture configuration.

### Using the model in a Kaggle Notebook

To play against the bot or run evaluations, use the `ChessAI` wrapper from the [GitHub repository](https://github.com/mateuszgrzyb-pl/searchless-chess).

```python
# 1. Add this model to your Kaggle Notebook
# 2. Install requirements: !pip install python-chess
# 3. Use the following code:

import chess
# Assuming you cloned the src from the GitHub repo
from src.chess_ai.core.model import ChessAI

# Path to the specific variation on Kaggle
MODEL_PATH = '/kaggle/input/searchless-chess/keras/vit-medium/1/model.keras'

chess_bot = ChessAI(MODEL_PATH)
board = chess.Board()

# Let the bot choose a move
engine_move = chess_bot.make_move(board)
print(f"Engine played: {engine_move}")
```

---

## 🔬 Architecture Details

### Vision Transformers (ViT-Small & ViT-Medium)
The model treats the chess board as a set of **64 tokens** (1x1 patches). It uses self-attention to understand global relationships simultaneously—allowing the model to "see" how a bishop on c1 affects the king on g8 without deep convolutional stacking.
- **ViT-Medium:** 8 Layers, 8 Heads, 256 Embedding Dim.
- **ViT-Small:** 5 Layers, 4 Heads, 256 Embedding Dim.

### ResNet-Large
A deep convolutional baseline with **10 residual blocks** and **256 filters**. It detects spatial patterns through convolutions. While powerful, it requires significantly more parameters than ViT to achieve similar ELO, highlighting the efficiency of the Transformer architecture in chess.

---

## 📂 Dataset
The models were trained on **316M deduplicated chess positions**.
Dataset available on Kaggle: **[Lichess Chess Positions: ML-Ready & Deduplicated](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/mateuszgrzybpl/lichess-chess-positions-ml-ready-and-deduplicated)**

## 📜 Citation & Research
This project was inspired by DeepMind's research on searchless chess. If you use these models, please cite:

Overview

This model performs image-based waste classification using a MobileNetV2 convolutional neural network trained on the TCV Waste Classification Dataset. The model was developed as part of an academic computer vision project focusing on lightweight deep learning for sustainable waste sorting systems.

The model classifies household waste into four categories:

• Glass
• Metal
• Paper
• Plastic

It is optimized for small real-world datasets and designed for fast inference on edge devices and mobile hardware.


Training Details

Architecture: MobileNetV2 (transfer learning)
Input resolution: 224 × 224 RGB
Training framework: TensorFlow / Keras
Optimizer: Adam
Loss: Sparse categorical cross-entropy
Preprocessing: OpenCV enhancement + data augmentation
Dataset: TCV custom dataset (2025)


Performance

The model achieved strong classification accuracy and macro F1-score on the test set, outperforming classical HOG+SVM and heavier CNN baselines in speed-to-accuracy tradeoff.

It is suitable for:

• real-time waste sorting prototypes
• smart recycling systems
• student AI projects
• mobile/embedded deployment
• lightweight edge inference


Usage Example (TensorFlow)

import tensorflow as tf
import numpy as np
from tensorflow.keras.preprocessing import image

model = tf.keras.models.load_model("model.h5")

img = image.load_img("sample.jpg", target_size=(224,224))
img_array = image.img_to_array(img) / 255.0
img_array = np.expand_dims(img_array, axis=0)

pred = model.predict(img_array)
class_names = ["Glass","Metal","Paper","Plastic"]
print(class_names[np.argmax(pred)])


Intended Use

This model is intended for research, education, and sustainability-focused AI development. It is not intended for commercial surveillance or harmful applications.


Author

Developed as part of a university computer vision research project (2025).

## Quickstart

> [!Important]
> Qwen3.5 models operate in thinking mode by default, generating thinking content signified by `<think>\n...</think>\n\n` before producing the final responses.


For streamlined integration, we recommend using Qwen3.5 via APIs. Below is a guide to use Qwen3.5 via OpenAI-compatible API. 
**Please refer the [git](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen3.5?tab=readme-ov-file#quickstart) for implementation purpose.**
## Best Practices

To achieve optimal performance, we recommend the following settings:

1. **Sampling Parameters**:
   - We suggest using `Temperature=0.6`, `TopP=0.95`, `TopK=20`, and `MinP=0` for thinking mode and using `Temperature=0.7`, `TopP=0.8`, `TopK=20`, and `MinP=0` for non-thinking mode.
   - For supported frameworks, you can adjust the `presence_penalty` parameter between 0 and 2 to reduce endless repetitions. However, using a higher value may occasionally result in language mixing and a slight decrease in model performance.

2. **Adequate Output Length**: We recommend using an output length of 32,768 tokens for most queries. For benchmarking on highly complex problems, such as those found in math and programming competitions, we suggest setting the max output length to 81,920 tokens. This provides the model with sufficient space to generate detailed and comprehensive responses, thereby enhancing its overall performance.

3. **Standardize Output Format**: We recommend using prompts to standardize model outputs when benchmarking.
   - **Math Problems**: Include "Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}." in the prompt.
   - **Multiple-Choice Questions**: Add the following JSON structure to the prompt to standardize responses: "Please show your choice in the `answer` field with only the choice letter, e.g., `"answer": "C"`."

4. **No Thinking Content in History**: In multi-turn conversations, the historical model output should only include the final output part and does not need to include the thinking content. It is implemented in the provided chat template in Jinja2. However, for frameworks that do not directly use the Jinja2 chat template, it is up to the developers to ensure that the best practice is followed.

5. **Long Video Understanding**: To optimize inference efficiency for plain text and images, the `size` parameter in the released `video_preprocessor_config.json` is conservatively configured. It is recommended to set the `longest_edge` parameter in the video_preprocessor_config file to 469,762,048 (corresponding to 224k video tokens) to enable higher frame-rate sampling for hour-scale videos and thereby achieve superior performance. For example,
    ```json
    {"longest_edge": 469762048, "shortest_edge": 4096}
    ```

    Alternatively, override the default values via engine startup parameters. For implementation details, refer to: [vLLM](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/34330) / [SGLang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/18467).

## Best Practices

To achieve optimal performance, we recommend the following settings:

1. **Sampling Parameters**:
   - We suggest using `Temperature=0.6`, `TopP=0.95`, `TopK=20`, and `MinP=0` for thinking mode and using `Temperature=0.7`, `TopP=0.8`, `TopK=20`, and `MinP=0` for non-thinking mode.
   - For supported frameworks, you can adjust the `presence_penalty` parameter between 0 and 2 to reduce endless repetitions. However, using a higher value may occasionally result in language mixing and a slight decrease in model performance.

2. **Adequate Output Length**: We recommend using an output length of 32,768 tokens for most queries. For benchmarking on highly complex problems, such as those found in math and programming competitions, we suggest setting the max output length to 81,920 tokens. This provides the model with sufficient space to generate detailed and comprehensive responses, thereby enhancing its overall performance.

3. **Standardize Output Format**: We recommend using prompts to standardize model outputs when benchmarking.
   - **Math Problems**: Include "Please reason step by step, and put your final answer within \boxed{}." in the prompt.
   - **Multiple-Choice Questions**: Add the following JSON structure to the prompt to standardize responses: "Please show your choice in the `answer` field with only the choice letter, e.g., `"answer": "C"`."

# Tiny Aya - Massively Multilingual Small Language Models

Cohere Labs Tiny Aya is an open weights research release of a 3.35 billion parameter model family optimized for efficient, strong, and balanced multilingual representation across 70+ languages, including many lower-resourced ones. The models are designed to support downstream adaptation, instruction tuning, and local deployment under realistic compute constraints.

**Developed by**: [Cohere](https://cohere.com/) and [Cohere Labs](https://cohere.com/research)

## Model Variants

This model family includes five variants available on Kaggle:

### Base (Pretrained Model)
- **Variant**: `base`
- **Type**: Pretrained foundation model
- **Use Case**: Base model for fine-tuning, and adaptation.
- **Kaggle Path**: `/kaggle/input/tiny-aya/transformers/base/1`

### Global (Chat Model)
- **Variant**: `global`
- **Type**: Instruction-tuned chat model
- **Optimization**: Best balance across languages and regions
- **Kaggle Path**: `/kaggle/input/tiny-aya/transformers/global/1`

### Earth (Chat Model)
- **Variant**: `earth`
- **Type**: Instruction-tuned chat model
- **Optimization**: Best for West Asian and African languages
- **Kaggle Path**: `/kaggle/input/tiny-aya/transformers/earth/1`

### Fire (Chat Model)
- **Variant**: `fire`
- **Type**: Instruction-tuned chat model
- **Optimization**: Best for South Asian languages
- **Kaggle Path**: `/kaggle/input/tiny-aya/transformers/fire/1`

### Water (Chat Model)
- **Variant**: `water`
- **Type**: Instruction-tuned chat model
- **Optimization**: Best for European and Asia Pacific languages
- **Kaggle Path**: `/kaggle/input/tiny-aya/transformers/water/1`

## Model Details

- **Model Size**: 3.35B parameters
- **Context Length**: 8K input, 8K output
- **Languages**: 70+ languages including English, Dutch, French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, Spanish, Czech, Polish, Ukrainian, Russian, Greek, German, Danish, Swedish, Norwegian, Catalan, Galician, Welsh, Irish, Basque, Croatian, Latvian, Lithuanian, Slovak, Slovenian, Estonian, Finnish, Hungarian, Serbian, Bulgarian, Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Turkish, Maltese, Hebrew, Hindi, Marathi, Bengali, Gujarati, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Tagalog, Malay, Indonesian, Vietnamese, Javanese, Khmer, Thai, Lao, Chinese, Burmese, Japanese, Korean, Amharic, Hausa, Igbo, Malagasy, Shona, Swahili, Wolof, Xhosa, Yoruba, and Zulu

## Model Architecture

This is an auto-regressive language model that uses an optimized transformer architecture. The chat models (global, earth, fire, water) use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and preference training to align model behavior to human preferences for helpfulness and safety.

The model features three layers with sliding window attention (window size 4096) and RoPE for efficient local context modeling and relative positional encoding. A fourth layer uses global attention without positional embeddings, enabling unrestricted token interactions across the entire sequence.

## Intended Usage

Tiny Aya is a family of massively multilingual small language models built to bring capable AI to languages that are often underserved by existing models. The models support languages across Indic, East and Southeast Asian, African, European, and Middle Eastern language families, with a deliberate emphasis on low-resource language performance.

**Intended applications include**:
- Multilingual text generation
- Conversational AI
- Summarization
- Translation and cross-lingual tasks
- Research in multilingual NLP and low-resource language modeling
- Efficient deployment in multilingual regions

## Strengths

Tiny Aya demonstrates strong open-ended generation quality across its full language coverage, with particularly notable performance on low-resource languages. The model performs well on translation, summarization, and cross-lingual tasks, benefiting from training signal shared across language families and scripts.

## Limitations

**Reasoning tasks**: The model's strongest performance is on open-ended generation and conversational tasks. Chain-of-thought reasoning tasks such as multilingual math (MGSM) are comparatively weaker.

**Factual knowledge**: As with any language model, outputs may contain incorrect or outdated statements, particularly in lower-resource languages with thinner training data coverage.

**Uneven resource distribution**: High-resource languages benefit from richer training signal and tend to exhibit more consistent quality across tasks. The lowest-resource languages in the model's coverage may show greater variability, and culturally specific nuance, sarcasm, or figurative language may be less reliably handled in these languages.

**Task complexity**: The model performs best with clear prompts and instructions. Highly complex or open-ended reasoning, particularly in lower-resource languages, remains challenging.
